::: {.why}
Three techniques cover most expectation problems asked in interviews, and recognising which one applies in the first fifteen seconds is what separates a two-minute answer from a ten-minute one.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Solve eight expectation problems under a clock, and for each name the technique before starting.
- State the recognition rule for each of the three techniques.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [40 min]{.task-min} Forty minutes, eight problems. Before starting each one, write down which technique you are going to use. Getting the technique right and the arithmetic wrong is a much better outcome than the reverse, and tracking the two separately tells you which to practise.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Write the three recognition rules: indicators when the quantity is a count of events, conditioning when the process has a natural first step, and symmetry when relabelling the objects leaves the problem unchanged. Then test the rules against the eight problems you just did.
:::
:::

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
A scored session with the technique predicted before each problem, and three written recognition rules.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
You draw cards until you see an ace. Expected number of draws? Do it by symmetry in under a minute.
:::
